predictions.title: Microsoft MAI coding model becomes the default GitHub Copilot engine by Q4 2026
predictions.body: Microsoft used its June 2 Build 2026 keynote to debut an in-house MAI model family that includes a coding-focused model explicitly positioned to power GitHub Copilot, its most direct move yet to reduce dependence on OpenAI for foundation-model capability. One day earlier, on June 1, GitHub flipped every Copilot plan to usage-based billing, replacing flat-rate premium requests with per-token GitHub AI Credits and removing the fallback that let users who exhausted their allowance drop to a cheaper model and keep working. These two events are halves of the same margin story: metered billing now exposes Microsoft's own gross margin on every agentic Copilot request, and a first-party model it does not pay OpenAI per-token for is the cleanest lever to protect that margin. The prediction is that within about two quarters Microsoft makes the MAI coding model the default engine behind GitHub Copilot's high-volume agentic paths — code completion, the autonomous bug/feature/PR agent, and chat — routing GPT-class models to a premium or opt-in tier rather than the standard path. Expect the shift to surface as Copilot release-note or changelog language naming a Microsoft first-party model as the default for Copilot completions or agent mode, distinct per-model token rates in the published GitHub AI Credits price table, and Build/Ignite messaging framing first-party inference as the cost engine under the new metered plans.

reasoning.because: Microsoft debuted an MAI coding model at Build 2026 positioned to power GitHub Copilot
reasoning.given: GitHub's June 1 per-token Copilot billing exposes Microsoft's margin on every OpenAI-paid request
reasoning.so_that: Microsoft routes Copilot's high-volume agentic paths to MAI by default and pushes GPT-class models to a premium tier
reasoning.landing: by Q4 2026; Copilot changelog names a first-party default + per-model rates
reasoning.plain_language: Microsoft now pays per use for GitHub Copilot, so it will quietly switch Copilot to its own cheaper coding model by default.

predictions.summary: Microsoft debuted an in-house MAI coding model at Build 2026 to power GitHub Copilot, a day after GitHub moved Copilot to per-token billing. By Q4 2026 Microsoft makes MAI the default engine for Copilot's high-volume agentic paths, pushing GPT-class models to a premium tier.

predictions.title: Snowflake ships a metered Claude-in-Cortex governed-data agent tier by Q4 2026
predictions.body: At the June 2 Snowflake Summit Platform Keynote, Snowflake announced direct integration of Anthropic's Claude into Cortex AI, extending the roughly $200M partnership the two signed in December and letting its 13,900+ enterprise customers run Claude-powered agents against governed data without that data leaving the platform. The keynote leaned hard on the compliance wedge — Daniela Amodei framing trust as a business accelerant, and named adopters Carvana, eSentire, and Notion anchoring the regulated-industry pitch. That framing only converts to revenue if Snowflake meters it: a December capability-partnership plus a named agent control plane (Snowflake Intelligence for knowledge workers, Cortex Code for engineers) is the setup for a consumption SKU, not a free feature. Snowflake's whole model is credit-based consumption, and a frontier-model agent running against governed tables is the highest-margin compute it can sell. Expect Snowflake to convert Claude-in-Cortex from a launch headline into a packaged, separately-metered governed-data agent tier — priced on Snowflake credits per agent run or per token, with the no-data-egress compliance story as the upsell justification for finance, healthcare, and public-sector buyers — and to report it as a named growth line. The GitHub Copilot move to per-token usage-based billing the day prior signals the same industry tilt: agentic AI capability is shifting onto metered consumption rather than flat-rate inclusion, and Snowflake's consumption-native pricing makes it the natural template for monetizing a hosted Claude agent.

reasoning.because: Snowflake integrated Claude into Cortex AI at its June 2 keynote, extending a ~$200M Dec partnership
reasoning.given: Snowflake prices on consumption credits; a governed-data frontier agent is its top-margin compute
reasoning.so_that: Snowflake converts Claude-in-Cortex into a separately-metered, compliance-positioned governed-data agent SKU
reasoning.landing: by Q4 2026; Snowflake pricing SKU + earnings-call consumption callout
reasoning.plain_language: Snowflake just put Claude into its data platform. Because it charges by usage, it will soon sell those AI agents as a paid, metered add-on.

predictions.summary: Snowflake integrated Anthropic's Claude into Cortex AI at its June 2 keynote, extending a ~$200M December partnership with a no-data-egress compliance pitch. Because Snowflake prices on consumption, expect it to package Claude-in-Cortex as a separately-metered governed-data agent tier by Q4 2026.

predictions.title: BadHost CVE-2026-48710 CVSS score gets upgraded above 6.5 by Q4 2026
predictions.body: The CVSS 6.5 base score assigned to BadHost (CVE-2026-48710), the Starlette host-header injection flaw, gets revised upward to high severity by Q4 2026, with either NVD re-scoring the record or downstream consumers publishing higher vendor-specific advisories. The disclosing researchers at X41 D-Sec and OSTIF have already gone on record that 6.5 understates the downstream impact: a single-character Host-header primitive defeats path-based authentication middleware and chains to authentication bypass, server-side request forgery, and in some cases remote code execution. The flaw sits under FastAPI's routing core at roughly 325 million weekly downloads and reaches the local-LLM serving stack — vLLM, LiteLLM, and MCP servers whose spec mandates unauthenticated OAuth discovery endpoints. That combination of mass deployment and clean escalation is exactly the profile that drives post-disclosure score inflation as exploitation paths get demonstrated in the wild and vendors who ship affected gateways issue their own advisories above the conservative initial rating.

reasoning.because: X41 and OSTIF publicly argue the initial CVSS 6.5 understates BadHost's RCE/SSRF escalation
reasoning.given: Starlette underpins FastAPI/vLLM/LiteLLM/MCP at ~325M weekly downloads with auth-bypass reach
reasoning.so_that: NVD re-scores CVE-2026-48710 to high severity or downstream vendors publish advisories above 6.5
reasoning.landing: by Q4 2026; NVD record edit or >=1 vendor advisory rating the flaw high
reasoning.plain_language: A bug in code that runs millions of AI servers got a low danger score, but experts say it is worse, so it will rise.

predictions.summary: X41 and OSTIF say BadHost's initial CVSS 6.5 understates a flaw chaining to auth bypass, SSRF, and RCE across Starlette, vLLM, LiteLLM, and MCP servers. Expect it revised to high severity by Q4 2026, via an NVD re-score or vendor advisories rating it above 6.5.
